children.text: With the NAFTA vote approaching, both sides were escalating pressure on Congress. President Clinton enlisted three former presidents to publicly endorse the treaty, while opponents, including Ross Perot and organized labor, continued building opposition. NPR reporter Richard Gonzales noted that Latino/as were playing critical roles on both sides, with New Mexico Congressman Bill Richardson leading pro-NAFTA efforts as chief deputy whip and California Congressman Esteban Torres leading opposition, though Torres indicated he might switch his vote if the administration committed to a North American Development Bank for border cleanup and worker retraining. In California, the state legislature approved a measure denying driver's licenses to undocumented immigrants, while rejecting bills that would have cut health and education services to the same group. Other approved bills required proof of legal residency for state-funded employment training and made immigrant smuggling a state crime. Latino/a legislators were divided on most measures. A federal health report found rising rates of AIDS and homicide among minority youth and stark health disparities along lines of race, education, and geography. In New York City, Mayor David Dinkins won the Democratic primary and was preparing for a close general election against Republican Rudolph Giuliani, with Latino/a voters seen as decisive. Radio Bilingüe in Fresno launched the first Spanish-language public-radio satellite network in the country, providing a new platform for Latino/a public-radio producers nationwide.

More than 250 chief executive officers of top Hispanic-owned companies gathered in Washington for a conference organized by Hispanic Business magazine, where they met with members of Congress and Clinton cabinet officials. Total revenues for Latino/a-owned businesses were reported at $34 billion and projected to reach $49 billion by 2000. A majority of attendees supported NAFTA, citing cultural and linguistic advantages in doing business with Mexico. However, many expressed concern that the Clinton healthcare plan, as outlined, could threaten the profitability of small and mid-size Latino/a businesses through mandatory coverage requirements. CEOs proposed tax incentives for small businesses as a mechanism to offset participation costs. Congresswoman Lucille Roybal-Allard noted that Congress was paying increasing attention to Latino/a business interests as the community's economic and political influence grew.

Latino USA's Franc Contreras and Patricia Guadalupe attended the annual Hispanic Heritage Awards gala in Washington. Actress Rita Moreno served as mistress of ceremonies, joined by Sesame Street's bilingual Muppet Rosita in a comedic exchange about the meaning of heritage. Award recipients included golfer Chi-Chi Rodriguez, Puerto Rican community educator Sister Isolina Ferre, playwright Luis Santeiro, National Council of La Raza president Raul Yzaguirre, and, in the music category, Gloria and Emilio Estefan. Sister Ferre called for educational programs that address school dropouts and literacy, as the foundation of real community development. Yzaguirre urged Latinos to build their own institutions to advocate effectively for their interests. Gloria Estefan spoke about her album Mi Tierra as a deliberate effort to bring traditional Cuban music to a global audience at a moment when she felt the timing was right, and described making it partly as a cultural gift for her son.
Dr. Guadalupe Rivera on Diego Rivera and Mexico

Maria Hinojosa spoke with Dr. Guadalupe Rivera, daughter of Mexican muralist Diego Rivera and historian, in Austin for the opening of a Rivera exhibition at the Mexic-Arte Museum. Dr. Rivera clarified that she was the daughter of Diego Rivera and his second wife, Lupe Marin, not Frida Kahlo. She described her father as proud of his Mexican identity and committed to art as a vehicle for communicating the history and struggles of the Mexican people rather than as a commercial commodity. Asked what Diego Rivera might have thought of NAFTA, she said he would not have been pleased, believing that each country needed to preserve its own identity and fearing that the agreement could erode Mexico's cultural distinctiveness.

Commentator Barbara Renaud Gonzalez offered a lyrical meditation on Mexican Independence Day and what it means for Mexicans, Mexican Americans, and all who carry the legacy of Father Miguel Hidalgo's 1810 Grito de Independencia. She reflected on the continuity between Hidalgo's call for mestizo courage and the daily realities of Mexican workers she sees in Texas, describing September 16th as a celebration of the ongoing, unfinished quest for the Mexican soul. The episode also captured the sounds of the grito ceremony held outside the Mexican consulate in Austin, where community members expressed pride in their culture and their place in the United States.
